Is the "smartphone" the key detail — i.e., the call is happening over a smartphone video/audio in a way that lets the father see or learn something (like the hostage's whereabouts or condition)?

Is the "hostage" an animal (a pet the family loves)?

Does refusing the ransom lead to the kidnapper being caught or exposed (so the daughter is freed)?

Does the father accept that the hostage may die (he chooses not to pay, knowing the hostage's life is at risk), prioritizing preventing his daughter from rushing into danger?
Does the daughter's pleading over the phone reveal to the father that she is determined to save the hostage (and would rush to the handover), prompting his decision?
Is the daughter already on her way to (or near) the hostage, so the father knows she will end up at any handover location?
Would the daughter be the one to physically carry/deliver the ransom money to the kidnapper (rather than the father himself)?
At the handover, would the daughter be harmed or killed (either by the kidnapper or by the trap)?
At the handover, would the daughter be taken captive by the kidnapper (becoming a second hostage)?
Would the daughter refrain from going to the handover if there is no ransom money to deliver (i.e., her plan depends on the payment being arranged)?
Does the father's refusal to pay prevent the daughter from going to the dangerous handover?
Is the scheduled handover the daughter's only way to find or reach the hostage/kidnapper location, so paying would give her a destination to rush to, while refusing denies her that?
Is it the father himself who physically prevents the daughter from going to the handover (e.g., he keeps her with him or stops her)?
Is the daughter safe (from the kidnapper's threat) after the father refuses to pay?
If the father refuses to pay, does the daughter still try to go to the kidnapper/handover anyway?
Is the reason paying would endanger the daughter that she would be the one delivering the money into the kidnapper's trap at the handover?
Would the hostage be killed at the handover trap regardless of the money (so paying cannot save the hostage)?
Is the father the "actual intended victim" in the sense that the whole extortion is designed to ruin him (his money and family) rather than to profit from a normal kidnapping?
Is the hostage the daughter's romantic partner (fiancé or boyfriend)?

The daughter is genuinely speaking and genuinely in danger, but she is not the hostage: the hostage is a separate person whom both she and her father care about (though apparently not her mother, nor her own child, nor a sibling). A real kidnapper is making the demand over the smartphone: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow or the hostage dies, with no police. The father cannot actually raise one hundred million yen by noon, but the decisive reason for his refusal is different.

The daughter is the one who would physically carry and deliver the ransom money to the kidnapper. The handover, however, is a trap — the act of delivering the money is exactly what endangers the hostage and, critically, the daughter. The father realizes that if the ransom were paid, the daughter would be the person sent to the handover and would walk straight into the lethal trap. The hostage would very likely die at that handover regardless, so payment could not save the hostage anyway.

The father's true priority is to protect his daughter: by refusing to pay, no handover is arranged and the daughter is kept out of the dangerous delivery. He knowingly accepts that the hostage may die as the cost of keeping his daughter from rushing into the kidnapper's trap. The scheme is really aimed at victimizing the father — through his money and his family — and he sees that cooperating (paying) is what would actually destroy him and endanger his daughter. So he decides the ransom should not be paid: paying would send his daughter into the trap and would not save the hostage, while refusing keeps her away from it.
